source.title: All Bark and No Bite: Rogue Dimensions in Transformer Language Models Obscure Representational Quality

record.tranche_reason: The study argues, based on its own experiments, that standard similarity measures in contextual language models can be dominated by a few dimensions and need qualification. It does not measure alignment between independently trained models or convergence with scale.
record.gate_note: The experiments measure within-model token similarity, its sensitivity to removing dimensions, and similarity to human lexical judgments. They do not measure cross-model convergence. Rows therefore use versions ["none"] and are described under fits_no_version. The authors also discuss Euclidean distance, but the retained Euclidean rows cover only selected final-layer conditions.
record.test_reason: The study analyses within-model geometry of four pretrained 768-d transformer LMs: anisotropy, how much a few rogue dimensions drive cosine and Euclidean similarity, the behavioural impact of ablating dimensions, and correlation with human word-similarity judgments after postprocessing. It never compares representations between models, seeds or modalities. It never measures alignment against scale, maps one model onto another, or matches features across models. Its metric-sensitivity point is about within-model similarity measures, not the metric dependence of cross-model convergence that V6 names. So it neither tests nor uses the claim. The record's T5 overstates the link: the paper makes no argument about any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that anisotropy is an artefact of rogue dimensions, not a global property of the space. They find rogue dimensions track position 0 and punctuation, and that final-layer lexical quality is preserved once these dimensions are corrected. They state that cosine similarity and Euclidean distance are uninformative unless rogue dimensions are accounted for.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines contextual embedding geometry and postprocessing; it does not reproduce or directly apply the original sources' cross-model convergence methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported cosine-similarity results vary with layer and with the number of removed dimensions. The authors also report that postprocessing outcomes depend on method: standardization generally improves human-judgment correlations, while all-but-the-top depends on the number of components removed.

fits_no_version.finding: In later layers, removing 1–5 high-contribution dimensions changes which token pairs are similar, and the size of the effect varies by model. Cosine r² at k=1: BERT-11 0.046, XLNet-12 0.028. GPT-2-11 stays high at 0.967 but drops to 0.352 at k=3.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within-model cosine similarity in contextual LMs is dominated by a small, model- and layer-specific set of rogue dimensions.

fits_no_version.finding: After removing 5 rogue dimensions, anisotropy and self-similarity become consistent across models and layers (Appendix A, Figures 4–6). The authors say the models' similar geometry is obscured by rogue dimensions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Apparent cross-model differences in embedding geometry can be artefacts of a few outlier dimensions.

fits_no_version.finding: Dimensions that dominate cosine similarity have little influence on the language-model output distribution, especially in GPT-2 and XLNet.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A dimension's contribution to similarity does not track its behavioural importance.

fits_no_version.finding: Standardization improves correlation with human word-similarity judgments in nearly all layers; the exception is early BERT layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Postprocessing choice alters measured lexical representational quality.

record.problems: The study does not test cross-model alignment, scaling, or capability, so it cannot establish whether convergence depends on metric choice. The main experiments use English Wikipedia and contextual language models of one stated dimensionality and depth. Some reported results are in figures, and the text gives no numerical uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 also reports k=5 values, which duplicate the displayed k=3 values, and includes other layer results; those were not separately extracted. Tables 3 and 5 report full layer-by-layer Euclidean and cosine results; only selected final-layer Euclidean values and selected cosine layers were retained. Additional detailed model-layer values for anisotropy are in Tables 1 and 4 and were not extracted because they do not measure cross-model convergence.

untested.parts: No cross-model comparison, and no scale or capability variation.
No seed comparisons. MultiBERTs are mentioned only as future work.
No mapping, stitching or relative representations between models.
Rogue dimensions tied to position 0 and '.' appear in all four models, but the paper does not match features across models.
Metric sensitivity is shown only for within-model token similarity, not for cross-model convergence.
No cross-model alignment level, plateau, or test of shared-data explanations.

record.verdict_notes: Nine cosine rows for GPT-2 and BERT carry Euclidean values (Table 3) instead of the Table 2/5 cosine values. As a result, the record's fits_no_version wrongly treats GPT-2-11 at k=1 as dominated and misses BERT's extreme cosine dominance. The study bears on no version; no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: No comparison of independently trained models, architectures, objectives, data, model scale, or capability.
No paired image-caption representations or vision-language alignment.
No comparison of seeds, shared features, or shared subspaces.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired alignment test.
No test of recurring interpretable features or circuits across models.
The study tests metric sensitivity for within-model token geometry, not metric dependence of cross-model convergence; it also does not test convergence out of distribution.
No test of cross-model alignment plateaus or whether shared data or objectives explain alignment.

rows.subject: GPT-2
rows.operation_detail: Ablate individual dimensions by setting layer-normalization parameters to zero and compare the resulting language-model distribution with the original.
rows.measure: Relative dimension influence on language-model distribution, measured by mean KL divergence, compared with relative cosine-similarity contribution
rows.baseline: Original language-model distribution
rows.value: Dimensions dominating cosine similarity cause only vanishingly small behavioral changes when ablated.
rows.note: The text explicitly describes the mismatch; it does not give a numerical KL value for these dimensions.
